title: Chapter I
focus: a privileged childhood and family love

teacherSummary.text: Victor describes his Genevese family: his father Alphonse, his mother Caroline (rescued from poverty), and the adopted Elizabeth Lavenza, whom his mother gives him as a 'present.' His childhood is loving and protected.

context.history: Geneva was an independent republic known for Calvinism and civic pride; Rousseau, a Genevan, influenced ideas of education and nature.

significance: Victor's ideal upbringing contrasts sharply with the creature's abandonment, raising the nature-versus-nurture question.
discussionQuestions: How does Victor's childhood compare with what a newly created being might need?

How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with creation and responsibility?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter I,” how does Shelley show a privileged childhood and family love? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter I develops the idea of a privileged childhood and family love. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and setting shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses characterization in Chapter I to complicate the reader's understanding of a privileged childhood and family love. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter I within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of a privileged childhood and family love responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter I as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of a privileged childhood and family love. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: How does Victor's childhood compare with what a newly created being might need? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include foldings, vagrants, decreasing, chamois, dungeons. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “During one of their walks a poor cot in the foldings of a vale attracted their notice, as being singularly disconsolate, while the number of half-clothed children gathered about it, spoke of penury in its worst shape.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: The act of making a fold or folds.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Geneva was an independent republic known for Calvinism and civic pride; Rousseau, a Genevan, influenced ideas of education and nature. Now, why does this chapter matter? Victor's ideal upbringing contrasts sharply with the creature's abandonment, raising the nature-versus-nurture question. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Setting, Foreshadowing.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot characterization, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.

She procured plain work; she plaited straw; and by various means contrived to earn a pittance scarcely sufficient to support life.
